To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
screening for colorectal adenomas and cancer by fecal occult blood testing (FOBT) and colonoscopy is effective in reducing CRC incidence and mortality.
screening for CRC by colonoscopy is effective and cost-effective and that it should be performed in all adults aged 50 years and older.
screening for CRC reduces mortality from this cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of colorectal cancer (cancer of the colon or rectum) at an earlier stage, and thus, the prevention of death from this disease.
the development and application of new technologies for the early detection and prevention of cancer.
the development of new methods for detecting and treating cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
screening for CRC is a public health success story.
CRC is a preventable disease.
the history of screening for CRC is a history of success and a model for other cancers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are now at the beginning of a new phase of screening, which will be characterized by more efficient, effective, and equitable methods, and by more complete eradication of CRC.
“the history of colorectal cancer screening is the story of a few people doing the right things at the right time.”

we were lucky to be in the right place at the right time, to work with a group of colleagues who were also lucky, and to be in a country that provided a supportive environment for research and implementation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can do a better job of educating patients about their risk for colorectal cancer, and we need to do more to help our patients understand their options for prevention and screening.
we need to be more aware of our own mortality.
screening is effective, but it must be performed with the right tools and by the right people.
